title: The Legal Sector: Is Judgement day here?
description: Send us Fan Mail Discover what happens when the unstoppable force of AI collides with the immovable object of the legal profession. Is it a game-changer for veteran attorneys yet a potential pink slip for junior staff? We delve into the legal industry's seismic transformation, showcasing how AI-powered tools like ROSS Intelligence and Case Text are revolutionizing workflows, while keeping a keen eye on the human touch—jury persuasion, strategic decisions, and client connections—that technology can't replace. In the second half of today's episode we welcome Kelly Inga, for a view from inside the industry. And for those working in the legal sector make sure to hang on to the very end of the podcast for a bang up to date list of new AI tools specifically designed for the legal sector. Finessing AI tools, a skill becoming as critical as the gavel in a courtroom. Our conversation traverses through the nitty-gritty of crafting effective AI prompts, sharing insights that are essential not just for legal eagles but professionals in any field. We then pivot to imagine a future where lawyers might wield AI as their co-counsel during live trials, and we highlight the egalitarian impact of AI on legal access, empowering David to take on Goliath in ways like never before. In an industry predicated on precision, we confront the specter of 'machine hallucination'—AI's propensity for inaccuracies that could undermine the very foundations of legal trust. The episode contemplates the ripple effects of such errors and the complex dance between embracing AI and safeguarding the sanctity of legal advice. As we unpack these themes, we're not just speculating—we're prepping for a future that's knocking on the courthouse door, ready to redefine the essence of legal practice and the shape of legal careers. Clickable links from the show: A Moral Backlash will probably slow down AGI (Geoffrey Miller) How AI will revolutionise the practice of Law (Brookings.edu) Generative AI and the Law (LexisNexis) The AI Divide (Outro song. Suno, Jimmy Rhodes, Matt Cartwright)
summary: The legal episode pits augmentation against elimination: Goldman Sachs estimates 44% of legal tasks can be automated, and tools like CoCounsel and Harvey are already doing research and discovery in minutes, but hallucinated citations (the $5,000 Levidow sanction) show why humans must sign off. Guest Kelly Inga describes in-house teams building 'legal operations' functions around AI — and one employer planning to replace commercial contract lawyers with playbook software — while both hosts see AI regulation itself as the sector's growth opportunity.
keyTalkingPoints: Goldman Sachs 2023: generative AI could automate up to 44% of legal tasks — partners gain productivity, juniors and paralegals face elimination
Tools: CoCounsel (CaseText), Westlaw Precision, Harvey, Robin AI and more; discovery that took weeks now takes minutes with expert prompting
Hallucination stakes: Levidow, Levidow & Oberman fined $5,000 after ChatGPT invented six cases; obscure domains (Connecticut land use) are worst
Kelly Inga: a legal operations team builds parameters so low-risk contracts generate automatically — but sophisticated clients keep humans essential
One employer's plan: replace commercial lawyers with playbook software, escalating to humans only when the playbook fails
Access to justice upside: one-click 1,000-word robocaller lawsuits; AI regulation, privacy and cybersecurity law flagged as growth areas

jimmy: Binned his ChatGPT subscription for Claude — more genuine conversations and fewer guardrails
Junior and paralegal roles are the ones that disappear; those already in the profession have a leg up
There will always be a human in the loop in law — AI biases are a hidden black box unlike visible human biases, so no AI judges
Of all professions covered, law is one where AI will create as much work as it eliminates
matt: Opened with copium (Brookings: AI cannot woo a jury) but the 44% tasks figure frames a sector split unevenly between winners and casualties
The 'someone to blame' principle keeps a human at the end of every AI workflow — but that human is signing off, not doing the work
Real-time trial-transcript AI feeding attorneys questions mid-testimony is a fascinating near-term use case
AI regulation is a call to action: lawyers must help write binding rules — a genuine bright spot for the profession
